items.title: Today's lesson
items.content:
Two spoons of sugar, in a **glass** and in a **jug** of lemonade, open the lesson: same sugar, different sweetness.

Salt in water turns “dilute” and “concentrated” into a number, **% m/m**; labels on a glucose drip, vinegar and a sanitizer bring in **% m/v** and **% v/v**. Three beakers of salt water define **saturated** solutions and **solubility**; syrup, soda and **solubility curves** show the effect of **temperature**.

Some pictures have a **second picture or animation**: show picture 1, ask, then click ›.

items.title: You already know
items.content:
• solute, solvent and solution; a solution is a homogeneous mixture

• finding a percentage of a quantity

• units of mass (g) and volume (mL); 1 L = 1000 mL

items.title: By the end, you can
items.content:
**1.** Calculate concentration as % m/m, % m/v and % v/v.

**2.** Interpret solubility and saturated solutions, including the effect of temperature.

**3.** Solve numericals on concentration and solubility.

**Step 1**

**Step 2**

Read the key idea. Then check the formula on each picture (pointers 3 and 4).

**Step 3: calculate with the class**

% m/m = 10 ÷ 100 × 100 = **10%**

**Step 4: calculate with the class**

% m/m = 10 ÷ 50 × 100 = **20%**. Same salt, half the solution: twice as concentrated.

items.prompt: 25 g of sugar is dissolved in 100 g of water. The concentration of the solution is
A talcum powder contains 4% m/m zinc oxide. How much zinc oxide is there in a 300 g tin?

items.text:
**On this question**

**A**: mass of solution = 25 + 100 = 125 g, so % m/m = 25 ÷ 125 × 100 = **20%**. Students who choose 25% divided by the mass of the water.

**On this question**

**B**: 4 g in every 100 g, so 4 × 3 = **12 g**.

items.prompt: A 500 mL bottle of saline is 0.9% m/v common salt. How much salt does it contain?
Two tablespoons (15 mL each) of orange juice concentrate are mixed with water to make a 150 mL glass of juice. The % v/v of the concentrate is

items.text:
**On this question**

**B**: 0.9 g in every 100 mL, so 0.9 × 5 = **4.5 g**.

**On this question**

**C**: volume of concentrate = 2 × 15 = 30 mL, so % v/v = 30 ÷ 150 × 100 = **20%**.

items.prompt: True or false? A saturated solution is always a concentrated solution.
options: True: it holds all it can dissolve
True: the two words mean the same
False: it has no solute left

items.prompt: At 30 °C, at most 15 g of a salt dissolves in 50 g of water. Its solubility at 30 °C in g per 100 g of water is

items.text:
**On this question**

**B**: false. A substance with a very low solubility makes a saturated solution with very little solute in it, so the solution is **dilute**.

**On this question**

**C**: twice the water dissolves twice as much: 15 × 2 = **30 g** per 100 g of water.

The solubility curves of potassium nitrate and common salt (sodium chloride). Read the axes with the class first.

**Answer to Question 16**

**Step 2. Potassium nitrate**: from 21 g at 10 °C to 167 g at 80 °C. Common salt hardly changes (36 g to 37 g).

**Answer to Question 17**

**Step 3. Common salt** (36 g, against 21 g of potassium nitrate). Now click › (pointer 4).

**Step 4: click › (now 2 of 3)**

**Step 5.** Students type their working in the box (pointer 6). 106 g at 60 °C, but only 32 g at 20 °C. The other 106 − 32 = **74 g** comes out of the solution as solid **crystals**. Now click › (pointer 7).

items.prompt: Why are bottles of soda kept cold until they are opened?
options: CO₂ is more soluble in cold water
CO₂ is less soluble in cold water
Cold glass lets less gas escape

items.prompt: A saturated solution of common salt in 100 g of water at 80 °C (37 g) is cooled to 20 °C (36 g). How much salt crystallises?

items.text:
**On this question**

**A**: carbon dioxide is **more soluble in cold water**, so more of it stays dissolved and the drink stays fizzy.

**On this question**

**A**: 37 − 36 = **1 g** only, because the solubility of common salt barely changes with temperature.
